'''Ashok Parthasarathi''' (1940–2019) was an Indian [[physicist]] and [[electronics engineer]] who served as a Science and Technology Advisor to [[Prime Minister of India|Prime Minister]] [[Indira Gandhi]].<ref name="wire" /> He played a crucial role in India's science and technology policies and helped the country become self-reliant in the field.<ref name=better>{{cite web|url=https://www.thebetterindia.com/196142/ashok-parthasarathi-self-reliance-science-technology-satellite-psu-tribute-india/|work=[[The Better India]]|author=Rinchen Norbu Wangchuk|title=Ashok Parthasarathi: The Man Who Helped Make India Self-Reliant in Science &Tech}}</ref> <!-- the site can't be reached using this link, try using the functioning link https://www.google.com/amp/s/www.thebetterindia.com/196142/ashok-parthasarathi-self-reliance-science-technology-satellite-psu-tribute-india/amp/ instead, which is however blocked by Wikipedia -->

He was the son of the diplomat [[Gopalaswami Parthasarathy (diplomat)|Gopalaswami Parthasarathy]], and the grandson of the civil servant and statesman [[N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar]].<ref name="better" />

==Life and career==
Parthasarathi did research in [[radio astronomy]] at the [[University of Cambridge]], [[UK]] with [[Martin Ryle]].<ref name="mainstream" /> He subsequently taught [[physics]] at the [[Birla Institute of Technology & Science, Pilani]]. Afterwards, he studied [[science policy]] at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]], US.<ref name="mainstream" /><ref name="better" />

From 1967 to 1970, Parthasarathi served as Special Assistant to [[Vikram Sarabhai]], the Chairman of the [[Atomic Energy Commission of India|Atomic Energy Commission]].<ref name="better" /> From 1970 to 1976, and again from 1980 to 1984, he was Special Assistant for Science and Technology to Prime Minister [[Indira Gandhi]]. He worked closely with Indira Gandhi's Principal Secretary [[P. N. Haksar]] to create the foundation for modern Indian science and technology.<ref name="better" /> He held important positions in the [[Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (India)|Department of Scientific and Industrial Research]], the Department of Electronics, and the [[Ministry of New and Renewable Energy]].<ref name="print" /><ref name="wire" />

Parthasarathi helped establish [[public sector enterprise]]s in the 1970s that would manufacture critical products such as [[microchip]]s and [[optic fibre]]s, at a time when India could not afford to import latest technologies.<ref name="better" />

He also was involved in defence matters, such as being consulted by the government during the [[1971 Indo-Pakistani War]], and playing a key role in the [[Smiling Buddha|1974 nuclear test in Pokhran]].<ref name="print" /><ref name="better" />

Following his retirement from the government in 2000, he wrote extensively on science policy;<ref name="better" /> he also served as a professor at the [[Centre for Studies in Science Policy]], [[Jawaharlal Nehru University]] from 2000 to 2005,<ref name="print" /> upon invitation.<ref name="mainstream" />

==Death==
A. Parthasarathi died after a period of illness at his residence in [[New Delhi]] on August 12, 2019, and was survived by his wife Vibha Parthasarathi, and sons Vibodh and Unmesh.<ref name="mainstream" />
